subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 7-year-old child with sickle cell disease develops fever and a sudden drop in hemoglobin from 9 to 5 g/dL during a parvovirus B19 illness. The reticulocyte count falls to near zero, but the white blood cell and platelet counts remain normal.
question: How does this episode differ from aplastic anemia?

options.text: Aplastic anemia also transiently arrests only the erythroid line, with normal platelets and neutrophils
Aplastic anemia is always caused by parvovirus B19
This child has pancytopenia, whereas aplastic anemia affects only red blood cells
Aplastic anemia has normal reticulocyte counts, unlike this episode
Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, whereas an aplastic crisis affects only the erythroid line

explanation_correct: Parvovirus B19 destroys erythroid progenitors and causes a pure red-cell aplastic crisis: anemia with reticulocytopenia but preserved neutrophils and platelets. Aplastic anemia is failure or destruction of hematopoietic stem cells and produces pancytopenia with anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, along with low reticulocytes and high EPO. Cell morphology remains normal, but the bone marrow is hypocellular with fatty infiltration. Causes include radiation, viruses, drugs, Fanconi anemia, and idiopathic immune-mediated disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aplastic anemia affects all three lineages, not just the erythroid line; this child's isolated anemia is an aplastic crisis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Parvovirus B19 causes aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemias; aplastic anemia has many causes and is not typically parvovirus-driven.
explanation_incorrect.C: The reverse is true: this child has isolated anemia, whereas aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Both aplastic anemia and aplastic crisis show low reticulocyte counts; the key distinction is the number of cell lineages affected.

educationalObjective: Distinguish aplastic crisis (pure erythroid arrest, often from parvovirus B19) from aplastic anemia (pancytopenia from stem cell failure).

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 9-year-old boy has short stature, cafe-au-lait spots, and absent thumbs with radial ray defects. CBC shows pancytopenia, and bone marrow biopsy is hypocellular. A sister was treated for a childhood malignancy.
question: Which underlying disorder best explains this presentation?

options.text: Down syndrome
Neurofibromatosis type 1
Fanconi anemia
Diamond-Blackfan anemia
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

explanation_correct: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair defect that causes progressive bone marrow failure and is a classic cause of aplastic anemia in childhood. Associated findings include short stature, cafe-au-lait spots, thumb or radial defects, and a predisposition to malignancy. The CBC may show normocytosis or macrocytosis, with pancytopenia, low reticulocytes, and a hypocellular fatty marrow on biopsy. Recognition matters because management can involve immunosuppression, androgens, or allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Down syndrome is associated with transient abnormal myelopoiesis and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, not the thumb/radial defects and DNA repair defect described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neurofibromatosis type 1 features cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, but not the thumb/radial aplasia or the classic inherited marrow failure syndrome in this vignette.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a congenital pure red-cell aplasia from a ribosomal protein defect; it causes anemia alone, not pancytopenia with radial anomalies.
explanation_incorrect.E: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal PIGA mutation causing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and thrombosis, not a congenital DNA repair syndrome.

educationalObjective: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive DNA repair defect causing aplastic anemia with short stature, cafe-au-lait spots, thumb/radial defects, and cancer predisposition.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 34-year-old agricultural worker develops fatigue, recurrent mouth infections, and easy bruising over several months. He reports daily occupational exposure to benzene-containing solvents. CBC shows pancytopenia, and marrow biopsy is hypocellular with fatty replacement.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's marrow failure?

options.text: Toxic marrow injury from an offending chemical agent
Autoimmune destruction of peripheral platelets only
Parvovirus B19-mediated erythroid progenitor destruction
Gain-of-function JAK2 mutation
Dietary selenium deficiency

explanation_correct: Benzene is a classic marrow toxin that can cause aplastic anemia by damaging hematopoietic stem cells; other culprits include chloramphenicol, alkylating agents, and antimetabolites. The result is pancytopenia with low reticulocytes, high EPO, and a hypocellular fatty marrow. Initial management is withdrawal of the offending agent, with antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporine, or allogeneic transplantation for severe disease. Identifying the exposure is crucial because removing it may allow marrow recovery.

explanation_incorrect.B: Isolated immune platelet destruction is immune thrombocytopenia and would not cause anemia, leukopenia, or a hypocellular marrow.
explanation_incorrect.C: Parvovirus B19 causes pure red-cell aplastic crisis with preserved neutrophils and platelets, not pancytopenia with a fatty marrow.
explanation_incorrect.D: JAK2 gain-of-function mutations drive polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms with increased blood counts, not marrow failure.
explanation_incorrect.E: Selenium deficiency is not a recognized cause of aplastic anemia; it is associated with cardiomyopathy and hypothyroidism.

educationalObjective: Benzene and certain drugs cause aplastic anemia through toxic stem cell injury; withdrawal of the offending agent is the first step in management.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 22-year-old woman has pallor, petechiae, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. CBC: hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, WBC 1.9 x 10^3/microL, platelets 28 x 10^3/microL, MCV 92 fL, reticulocyte count 0.1%. Serum erythropoietin is markedly elevated. Bone marrow aspirate is hypocellular with fatty infiltration and normal cell morphology.
question: Which pathophysiologic mechanism best accounts for these findings?

options.text: Sequestration of antibody-coated red cells in the spleen with compensatory marrow hyperplasia
Impaired GPI-anchor synthesis causing complement-mediated red cell lysis
Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin due to deficient NADPH production
Failure or destruction of hematopoietic stem cells with inadequate marrow output
Hepcidin-mediated iron trapping caused by chronic inflammation

explanation_correct: The combination of pancytopenia, reticulocytopenia, elevated EPO, normal cell morphology, and a hypocellular fatty marrow is diagnostic of aplastic anemia. The primary defect is failure or destruction of hematopoietic stem cells from radiation, viral infection, drugs, Fanconi anemia, or idiopathic immune-mediated injury. Because marrow output is low, reticulocytes are decreased despite high EPO. The marrow is replaced by adipose tissue rather than being hypercellular, as would be expected in a hemolytic anemia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Extravascular autoimmune hemolysis shows spherocytes and a hypercellular marrow with isolated anemia, not pancytopenia with a fatty marrow.
explanation_incorrect.B: Defective GPI anchors cause paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria with intravascular hemolysis and thrombosis, not hypocellular marrow failure.
explanation_incorrect.C: NADPH deficiency causes G6PD deficiency with Heinz bodies and bite cells after oxidant stress, not pancytopenia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hepcidin excess produces anemia of chronic disease with iron trapping and high ferritin; it does not cause leukopenia or thrombocytopenia.

educationalObjective: Aplastic anemia is hypocellular marrow failure with pancytopenia, low reticulocytes, and high EPO, not a hemolytic or iron-handling disorder.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 30-year-old man has severe idiopathic aplastic anemia with hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, neutrophils 300/microL, and platelets 15 x 10^3/microL. He is transfusion-dependent, and no matched sibling donor has been identified immediately.
question: Which of the following is an accepted treatment approach for this condition?

options.text: Splenectomy alone
Immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine, with allogeneic transplantation as a potentially curative option
Eculizumab targeting complement protein C5
Hydroxyurea to increase fetal hemoglobin
Chronic oral iron supplementation

explanation_correct: Severe aplastic anemia is treated by removing any offending agent, using immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin plus cyclosporine for immune-mediated disease, and pursuing allogeneic bone marrow or stem cell transplantation, which can be curative, especially in younger patients with a matched donor. Supportive care includes red cell and platelet transfusion and marrow stimulation with GM-CSF. Because the defect is immune destruction or loss of stem cells, splenectomy, iron, or complement blockade does not restore hematopoiesis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Splenectomy helps in hereditary spherocytosis and some immune cytopenias; marrow failure in aplastic anemia is not due to splenic sequestration.
explanation_incorrect.C: Eculizumab blocks C5 in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and does not restore hematopoiesis in aplastic anemia, even though the diseases may coexist.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hydroxyurea induces fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease; it is not a therapy for hypocellular marrow failure.
explanation_incorrect.E: Oral iron is ineffective because iron stores are usually normal or increased and the problem is absent stem-cell output, not iron deficiency.

educationalObjective: Aplastic anemia therapy: remove the cause, use antithymocyte globulin/cyclosporine or allograft, and add transfusion support and GM-CSF as needed.
